title: THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS
body:
A. K. Dewdney's *The New Turing Omnibus*: 66 short chapters, each one a self-contained tour of a
single idea in computing, in no particular order and with no prerequisites between them. Theory
sits next to hardware sits next to graphics on purpose.

**Nobody reads it in order, so this parent is not organised by chapter.** It is organised by
which course in the degree each chapter feeds, because that is how the notes below actually get
used: the Omnibus is where a topic gets its short, motivated version before or after some course
gives it the long one. Evan's original chapter list is kept verbatim at the bottom.

This is the only folder in the vault that is not a course, and it is the one that ties the
others together. Almost every note here is a hub with links into two or three different course
folders.

## Computability and formal languages

The largest block, and it is [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613) in miniature. The
machines themselves live in that folder; these notes own the classification and the limits.

- [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] is the organising table for the whole subject: four classes of
  [[Languages]] nested strictly inside one another, each defined by a grammar shape, a machine,
  and a memory model at the same time.
- [[Regular Languages]] is the bottom rung, the class a finite amount of memory can decide. It
  is about the class, not the machines; [[DFA]], [[NFA]], [[Regular Expressions]], and
  [[Pumping Lemma]] own those.
- [[Nondeterminism]] asks the question the ladder keeps asking: does letting a machine guess buy
  any real power? For finite automata no, for [[Turing Machine]]s no, for [[NP-Complete]] nobody
  knows.
- [[Automata]] is the machine ladder as an index, over in COMP 2613.
- [[Turing Machine]] is the central object of that course and lives there, not here.
- [[Godel's Theorem]] is the logic half of [[Undecidability]]: a true statement the system cannot
  prove, built by the same self-reference trick five years earlier.
- [[Systems of Logic]] is the setup for it. Formal system = symbols, axioms, inference rules,
  with the propositional / first-order / arithmetic ladder and the sound-versus-complete
  distinction that Gödel's two theorems are constantly confused across.
- [[Simulation]] carries both senses of the word: one machine imitating another (the workhorse
  proof technique) and modelling a real system numerically. The note keeps them apart deliberately.

## Data structures and algorithms

Feeds [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]. Each of these is
a map over notes that live in those folders, plus one argument the individual notes do not carry.

- [[Search Trees]] is the family note: every [[Tree]] whose shape encodes an ordering.
  [[Binary Search Tree]] owns the invariant, [[Balanced Tree]] owns rotations, [[Heap]] owns the
  one member that is not a search tree, [[Hashing]] is the alternative that gives up order.
- [[Sequential Sorting]] maps [[Bubble Sort]], [[Insertion Sort]], [[Merge Sort]], and
  [[Quick Sort]], and carries the argument none of them do: **why $n \log n$ is a wall** for
  comparison sorting.
- [[Minimum Spanning Tree]] is the classic greedy result on a [[Weighted Graph]]: connect every
  vertex, no cycles, least total weight, and the greedy choice is provably optimal.
- [[Game Trees]] is search where an opponent is choosing half the moves. Minimax, the $O(b^d)$
  explosion, alpha-beta pruning, and the static evaluation function that every real engine
  needs because the tree never finishes.
- [[Algorithm]] and [[Asymptotic Analysis]] are the first-year and second-year notes this block
  assumes; [[Recursion]] likewise.

## Hardware and digital logic

Feeds [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) and [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659).

- [[Karnaugh Maps]] is the graphical minimisation method: Gray-code the axes so that algebraic
  cancellation becomes visible adjacency, group in powers of two, read off the terms. Fewer
  terms is fewer gates.
- [[Boolean Algebra]] holds the identities it is built on, and [[Digital circuit]],
  [[Combinational Logic]], [[Encoder]], [[Multiplexer]], and [[Decoder]] are what gets minimised.
- [[Error Correcting Code]] is the middle rung of the vault's three-rung error story:
  [[Error Detection]] notices, this repairs, [[Finite Field]] explains why the algebra works.
  Hamming codes for single bits, Reed-Solomon over $GF(2^8)$ for whole [[Byte]]s, and it is what
  a CD, a QR code, and a RAID array are all quietly doing.

## Numerical and graphical methods

Feeds the MATH block, mostly [[CALCULUS 1]] and [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]].

- [[Spline Curves]]: chain low-degree polynomials instead of fitting one high-degree one, because
  high-degree polynomials oscillate. Cubic is the smallest degree that reaches $C^2$ continuity,
  the solve is a tridiagonal system, and Bezier curves are the graphics-facing version behind
  every font outline and easing function.
- [[Random Numbers]]: a deterministic machine cannot produce randomness, so `rand()` returns a
  fully determined sequence that passes statistical tests. Same seed, same sequence, and that
  reproducibility is what makes [[Simulation]] debuggable. The cryptographic bar is higher, which
  is [[Stream Cipher]] in [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]].
- [[Cryptography]] is a pointer note. The book gives it one chapter; MATH 4111 gives it a term,
  so [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] holds the material and this note only records what the chapter covered.

## Neural networks and vision

The largest block by note count, written jointly with [[MACHINE LEARNING]] because the material
is one topic split across two folders. The Omnibus chapter is a 1989 introduction to the
[[Perceptron]]; everything downstream of it is modern.

- [[Neural Network]] is the hub: [[Neuron]], [[Input Layer]], [[Hidden Layer]], [[Output Layer]],
  [[Weights]], [[Bias Term]].
- [[Perceptron]] and [[Multilayer Perceptron]]: the single unit, why it cannot do XOR, and what a
  hidden layer fixes.
- [[Forward Pass]] **is** matrix multiplication, which is where [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] cashes out.
  [[Back Propagation]] is the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] run backwards, and
  [[Gradient Descent]] is [[Optimization]] with too many variables to solve directly.
- [[Activation Function]] and the reason for it, [[Non-Linear]]: [[Sigmoid]], [[ReLU]],
  [[Leaky ReLU]].
- [[Loss Function]] and [[Log Loss]], with [[Logistic Regression]] as the smallest model that
  needs gradient descent at all.
- [[CNN]] and [[Convolutional Neural Network]] for images, and [[Computer Vision]] for the
  problem they solve: an image is a [[Matrix]] of intensities and there is no formula from pixels
  to meaning.

## Core Facts to Know

- The book is 66 unordered self-contained chapters; the notes here are indexed by course, not by
  chapter number.
- The [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] defines each language class three ways at once: grammar, machine, memory.
- [[Godel's Theorem]] and [[Undecidability]] are the same result in two vocabularies, 1931 and 1936.
- First-order logic is **complete**; arithmetic is **incomplete**. Both are Gödel's and they are
  about different things.
- Comparison sorting cannot beat $n \log n$, because $n!$ orderings need $\log_2(n!)$ comparisons
  to distinguish.
- A spanning tree of $V$ vertices always has exactly $V - 1$ edges.
- A game tree is $O(b^d)$; alpha-beta returns the identical answer in $O(b^{d/2})$ with good move
  ordering.
- Minimisation on a K-map works because Gray-code adjacency means "differs in one variable".
- Detection needs Hamming distance $\ge 2$; correcting $t$ errors needs $\ge 2t + 1$.
- Reed-Solomon corrects whole symbols, not bits, which is what makes it survive scratches.
- Cubic is the lowest polynomial degree that gives $C^2$ continuity at the knots.
- Pseudo-random means fully determined and statistically indistinguishable, and the two halves of
  that are separately important.
- A [[Forward Pass]] is matrix multiplication; [[Back Propagation]] is the chain rule; neither is
  new mathematics.
- Two notes here are deliberately pointers rather than treatments: [[Cryptography]] hands off to
  MATH 4111, and [[Turing Machine]] was moved into COMP 2613 where it belongs.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613): the theory block above is this course's
  material, arrived at from the book's side.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: trees, sorting,
  graphs, and the complexity arguments over them.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) and [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659): logic
  minimisation, and the detection end of the error story.
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) and [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111): [[Finite Field]] is the
  algebra under [[Error Correcting Code]], and [[Post-Quantum Cryptography]] turns decoding back
  into a hardness assumption.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]]: the neural-network block, and
  [[Game Trees]] is the classical-AI chapter that predates all of it.
- [[CALCULUS 1]], [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]], [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]],
  [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]: splines, gradients, and the matrix view of a network.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) and [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271): [[Probability]] under random
  number generation, [[Proof]] under the logic block.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633): [[Recursion]] and [[Algorithm]], which
  nearly everything here assumes.
